a6248.speech: Said on Monday that emergency funding to help hundreds of thousands of refugees in Uganda will run out next month unless more support comes in, and that a funding crisis is threatening programmes for people fleeing there from strife-torn countries in the region including Sudan, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of Congo; said it would only be able to meet a third of the costs associated with supporting Sudanese refugees in Uganda and would have to cut its monthly funding to $5 per refugee from $16 unless more money is found; added that malnutrition rates are rising as food, water and medicine supplies shrink, while the risk of suicide is increasing among young refugees due to a reduction in mental health staff.

a6248.speaker: Dominique Hyde, UNHCR Director for External Relations
a6248.name: Dominique Hyde
a6248.title: UNHCR Director for External Relations
a6248.speech: Said in a statement: “Emergency funding runs out in September” ; “More children will die of malnutrition, more girls will fall victim to sexual violence, and families will be left without shelter or protection unless the world steps up.”

a6439.speaker: Kuwait News Agency (KUNA)
a6439.name: Kuwait News Agency (KUNA)
a6439.speech: Reported that the Kuwait Institute for Scientific Research and the CentraleSupélec group and the University of Perpignan signed a memorandum of understanding to establish a solar-powered water desalination project, while the two sides agreed to extend the memorandum of understanding signed between the Public Authority for Applied Education and Training and the Academy of Paris.

a6439.speaker: Laurent Fabius, French Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Development
a6439.name: Laurent Fabius
a6439.title: French Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Development
a6439.speech: Affirmed during his meeting last night with Kuwaiti Finance Minister Anas Al-Saleh his country's readiness to raise the level of economic cooperation and trade exchange with Kuwait, after France began a policy of economic diplomacy and the expansion of the French Foreign Ministry's powers to include the Ministry of Trade.

a6439.speaker: Kuwaiti Ministry of Finance (press statement)
a6439.name: Kuwaiti Ministry of Finance (press statement)
a6439.speech: A press statement by the Ministry of Finance quoted Minister Fabius confirming the growing economic and commercial relations between his country and Kuwait, pointing to the interest of the accompanying business delegation — which included a number of officials from the federation of major French companies and the French business agency — in a number of projects in Kuwait.

a6439.speaker: Anas Al-Saleh, Kuwaiti Finance Minister
a6439.name: Anas Al-Saleh
a6439.title: Kuwaiti Finance Minister
a6439.speech: Explained that the resumption of the joint Kuwaiti-French ministerial committee in Paris in February of last year contributed to raising the rate of trade exchange, and praised the French government's decision to grant travel visas to Kuwaiti citizens within 48 hours, the fastest visa France grants anywhere in the world.

a6517.speaker: Muyi Aina, Executive Director of the National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA)
a6517.name: Muyi Aina
a6517.title: Executive Director of the National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA)
a6517.speech: Said in an interview with the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) in Abuja on Sunday that the Nigerian government has disbursed more than N192 billion to strengthen primary healthcare facilities across Nigeria since the Basic Health Care Provision Fund (BHCPF) began disbursements in 2019 ; said that currency fluctuations and rising service costs continued to strain Nigeria's health system, even as budget allocations are increasing at both federal and state levels ; said that out-of-pocket expenditure still accounted for a disproportionate share of healthcare spending, with the public sector's contribution at just 14 per cent ; according to him, the government has mobilised N3.5 billion, 60 per cent of which is pooled from mechanisms such as the BHCPF, Global Fund, Gavi, and PEPFAR, mobilised through the Sector-Wide Approach (SWAp) and the Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative ; said that 8,309 facilities nationwide now receive quarterly funds under the BHCPF: “Allocations were recently scaled up from an average of N300,000 to between N600,000 and N800,000 per quarter, depending on facility size and patient volume.” ; “The reform, dubbed BHCPF 2.0, is designed to address real operational costs at the facility level, supporting human resources, essential commodities and infrastructure.” ; “Even though budget allocations are growing, the cost of healthcare delivery, vaccines, TB medicines, malaria commodities, and operational programmes is rising even faster.”

a6517.speaker: Muyi Aina, Executive Director of the NPHCDA
a6517.name: Muyi Aina
a6517.title: Executive Director of the NPHCDA
a6517.speech: Expressed government's commitment to closing existing financing gaps through stronger co-financing at the federal, state and local government levels, coupled with performance-based accountability measures, and said the federal government is set to roll out a direct funding mechanism across the country to improve accountability in healthcare spending: “The model, already piloted in four to five states, allows payments for commodities and health worker salaries to be made directly into designated accounts, making the process transparent and traceable. These are the sorts of things we are trying to do to ensure that funds reach their targets without leakages.”

a6517.speaker: Muyi Aina, Executive Director of the NPHCDA
a6517.name: Muyi Aina
a6517.title: Executive Director of the NPHCDA
a6517.speech: Said that government's analysis showed that between 15 per cent and 25 per cent of non-campaign vaccines in Nigeria cannot be accounted for, and that the losses could stem from wastage, inaccurate population estimates, procurement inefficiencies or weaknesses in vaccine management systems ; said that further state-level analysis is underway to close the accountability gap ; noted that the federal government is investigating discrepancies in vaccine utilisation across several sub-national units, with some reportedly consuming up to four times more vaccines than their recorded coverage rates, and that while border states may vaccinate non-Nigerian citizens, the scale of discrepancies points to deeper issues of accountability, wastage or faulty forecasting: “We are now telling states to go down to the local government level, identify where the problems are and fix them.” ; said that through efficiency measures the government had reduced projected vaccine procurement costs for the next five years from $1.5 billion to $1 billion.

a6607.speaker: Economic and political science experts (webinar organised by the Political Science Association)
a6607.name: Economic and political science experts (webinar organised by the Political Science Association)
a6607.speech: Said the withdrawal of aid by countries such as the United Kingdom and United States is a watershed moment for Malawi to rethink donor dependency ; argued that Malawi must brace for a world of reduced or no aid at all and thus begin to generate its own resources and manage them better to sustain its expenditure and citizens' well-being.

a6607.speaker: Dan Banik, professor of political science and research director at the University of Oslo, Norway
a6607.name: Dan Banik
a6607.title: professor of political science and research director at the University of Oslo, Norway
a6607.speech: Making a presentation titled 'Turning the tide: Political economy of aid in the context of recent shifts in US and UK policies', said looking ahead the picture looks gloomy for Malawi with aid uncertainty hanging over sectors such as education, health and pandemics: “Malawi will be one of the hardest hit countries due to the aid freeze. And this will result in economic instability and debt distress. I doubt if Europe will fill the gap. So, will Malawi and others get more aid from China?” ; doubted if the country can recover with current policies and economic trajectory, suggesting: “Leaders will need to take the right steps, including making tax collection more efficient. But most importantly Malawi must prioritise investing in areas such as agriculture or education and not what donors have been prioritising in the past.”

a6607.speaker: Bertha Bangara Chikadza, University of Malawi-based economist and head of the Economics Association of Malawi
a6607.name: Bertha Bangara Chikadza
a6607.title: University of Malawi-based economist and head of the Economics Association of Malawi
a6607.speech: Observed that for the past seven years, the country has been witnessing a drop in aid, but leaders never thought US support would dry up ; suggested robust measures such as an end to spot fines to deal with corruption and formalising the informal sector so that government boosts its revenue collection ; “Minus aid, the country should prioritise development. Sometimes we think we are entitled to aid. But we are not. Moves to boost tourism, mining and agriculture should be done on a large scale to generate local resources. It is high time we fixed the local revenue base.”

a6607.speaker: Limbani Nsapato, educationist
a6607.name: Limbani Nsapato
a6607.title: educationist
a6607.speech: Decried dependency on foreign aid, saying solutions to wean off dependency have been proposed, but largely ignored by politicians.

a6607.speaker: Moses Kunkuyu, Minister of Information and Digitisation of Malawi
a6607.name: Moses Kunkuyu
a6607.title: Minister of Information and Digitisation of Malawi
a6607.speech: Efforts to get his views proved futile yesterday, but he recently told The Guardian (UK) that being a repetitive victim of natural disasters and global economic woes, it is clear that Malawi still needs aid to get out of poverty.

a6607.speaker: Simplex Chithyola Banda, Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs of Malawi
a6607.name: Simplex Chithyola Banda
a6607.title: Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs of Malawi
a6607.speech: Said that in the 2025/26 fiscal year grants are estimated at K1.14 trillion, of which K1.10 trillion will come from international organisations and K86.36 billion from foreign governments.

a6607.speaker: Simplex Chithyola Banda, Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs of Malawi
a6607.name: Simplex Chithyola Banda
a6607.title: Minister of Finance and Economic Affairs of Malawi
a6607.speech: Said yesterday during his closing statement in Parliament that following the USAid decision, government will ensure that all services regarding HIV and Aids continue being offered in the country's health system, including treatment.

a6607.speaker: National Planning Commission
a6607.name: National Planning Commission
a6607.speech: Said that in the implementation of the MIP 1, which spans from 2020 to 2030, government's preference for development aid is grants and concessional loans, with the latter only contracted for projects with high rates of return and huge multiplier effects as part of accelerating the country's development agenda.

a6666.speaker: Rune Skinnebach, EU Ambassador to Malawi
a6666.name: Rune Skinnebach
a6666.title: EU Ambassador to Malawi
a6666.speech: Said the European Union will continue providing direct budget support to Malawi despite the recent cancellation of the IMF's Extended Credit Facility, but that the absence of the IMF programme will make implementation more challenging; told Times Radio's Kulinji Programme on Tuesday that while an IMF programme is not a condition for the EU's budget support it significantly helps with implementation and monitoring, and that the EU's budget support relies on many of the same criteria as the IMF's ECF, including public finance management, macroeconomic stability, debt restructuring, revenue mobilization and fiscal discipline: "An IMF ECF is not conditionality for our programme, but it is definitely helping it. It will make it much more difficult to maintain the full variable tranches in the absence of an IMF programme. We have variable tranches that are due to come at the end of this year and next year, and they depend on a series of criteria. The fact that we have the ECF made it much easier for us to launch the budget support." ; noted that despite the ECF cancellation the IMF will continue Article IV consultations with Malawi, maintaining discussions on the macroeconomic framework that forms the main requirement for EU budget support.

a6666.speaker: Rune Skinnebach, EU Ambassador to Malawi
a6666.name: Rune Skinnebach
a6666.title: EU Ambassador to Malawi
a6666.speech: Outlined a fundamental shift in the EU's approach to development partnerships, moving away from the traditional donor-beneficiary relationship toward investment-based collaboration: "The old donor-beneficiary relationship has proven to be unsustainable. The EU's Global Gateway initiative launched in 2022, mobilizes EUR 300 billion in investments, with half designated for Africa. Unlike traditional aid, these funds will be provided as concessional loans, investment leverage, and guarantees rather than grants." ; warned: "It is an offer that is up to the government of Malawi to take, to make sure that Malawi is attractive for investments. If it's not, then the investments will go elsewhere."

a6666.speaker: Ivy Nkhata, political scientist
a6666.name: Ivy Nkhata
a6666.title: political scientist
a6666.speech: Raised concerns over aid dependency creating a cycle of corruption and the need for greater alignment between donor priorities and Malawian aspirations, calling for greater participation by ordinary Malawians in aid discussions and more accountability from donors to ensure aid serves genuine local needs rather than imposed agendas: "Our reliance on foreign aid has created this vicious cycle of dependency and corruption in Malawi. Aid for so long has fueled corruption as the government tends to prioritise the donor system over public welfare. We want to see how the EU and other partners justify certain aid and ensure they are accountable to the people of Malawi as a whole, not just the political leaders they deal with."

a6666.speaker: Betchani Tchereni, Secretary to the Treasury of Malawi
a6666.name: Betchani Tchereni
a6666.title: Secretary to the Treasury of Malawi
a6666.speech: Dismissed concerns about the IMF ECF cancellation, saying Malawi has access to funding from other sources beyond traditional Western donors, and told the media that Malawi's relationship with the IMF remains intact despite the ECF cancellation.

a6752.speaker: Bloomberg (financial news agency)
a6752.name: Bloomberg (financial news agency)
a6752.speech: According to Bloomberg, USAID contractor companies and non-governmental organisations have warned officials that there are already banks refusing loans because of the suspension of these entities' operations, following the freeze on operations decreed by the new US President, Donald Trump.

a6752.speaker: USAID contractor companies and NGOs
a6752.name: USAID contractor companies and NGOs
a6752.speech: Warned officials that there are already banks refusing loans because of the suspension of their operations following the freeze decreed by President Donald Trump.

a6752.speaker: Humanitarian activists (documents filed in a US court)
a6752.name: Humanitarian activists (documents filed in a US court)
a6752.speech: Say, according to documents filed in a US court, that beyond the possibility of legal proceedings, workers are also facing physical threats over unpaid debts in the places where USAID was funding operations.

a6752.speaker: Democracy International (USAID implementing entity)
a6752.name: Democracy International (USAID implementing entity)
a6752.speech: Said it is facing lawsuits abroad if it cannot pay this month's salaries, notably in Tunisia, where 17 employees have joined together to claim their wages through the courts; said it owes three million dollars for services provided before 24 January, and has dismissed all 95 of its employees in the United States, now facing the risk of eviction from its headquarters and considering judicial liquidation.

a6752.speaker: Eric Bjornlund, head of Democracy International (declaration to the court)
a6752.name: Eric Bjornlund
a6752.title: head of Democracy International (declaration to the court)
a6752.speech: "In Tunisia, for example, our employees are being threatened by creditors with physical violence if they do not pay," wrote Eric Bjornlund in a declaration to the court, concluding that the employees "risk being arrested or attacked because of their close connection with USAID programmes that suddenly stopped keeping promises and honouring their obligations".

a7023.speaker: Aicha Farah, Director-General of the Centre for the Training of Basic Education Teachers (CFEEF), Djibouti
a7023.name: Aicha Farah
a7023.title: Director-General of the Centre for the Training of Basic Education Teachers (CFEEF), Djibouti
a7023.speech: In remarks made at the end of the ceremony, welcomed the initiative and encouraged the parents of the parents' associations (APE) and the teaching teams to promote reading further among their children in their schools and in their respective neighbourhoods.

a7023.speaker: Parents attending the reading festival
a7023.name: Parents attending the reading festival
a7023.speech: The parents present were all delighted with this initiative.

a7338.speaker: World Food Programme
a7338.name: World Food Programme
a7338.speech: Plans to deliver more than 17,000 tonnes of food products to support 1.5 million people for one month; announced the arrival of more than 700 trucks of food aid in the worst-affected areas.

a7338.speaker: International press
a7338.name: International press
a7338.speech: According to the international press, this convoy constitutes one of the first substantial aid deliveries since the start of the conflict.

a7338.speaker: The international community, especially the United States
a7338.name: The international community
a7338.title: especially the United States
a7338.speech: Is calling for unimpeded humanitarian access in order to reduce the suffering of civilian populations.

a7356.speaker: Elias Mpedi Magosi, SADC Executive Secretary
a7356.name: Elias Mpedi Magosi
a7356.title: SADC Executive Secretary
a7356.speech: In his opening remarks, welcomed the delegations and expressed gratitude to Madagascar for its hospitality.

a7356.speaker: Elias Mpedi Magosi, SADC Executive Secretary
a7356.name: Elias Mpedi Magosi
a7356.title: SADC Executive Secretary
a7356.speech: underscored the importance of unity among member states, particularly in the face of global economic headwinds: “We must remain united as we address the economic challenges brought about by rising tariffs and shifting geopolitical dynamics.”

a7356.speaker: SADC Council of Ministers
a7356.name: SADC Council of Ministers
a7356.speech: Ministers highlighted that regional self-reliance depended on stronger value chains and collaborative investment in manufacturing capacity, with strong emphasis on reducing dependency on raw commodity exports through industrialisation and value addition.

a7356.speaker: Eswatini’s delegation
a7356.name: Eswatini’s delegation
a7356.speech: actively contributed to the talks, voicing support for policies that advance competitiveness and expand cross-border trade.

a7356.speaker: Dr. Thambo Gina, Eswatini Minister for Economic Planning and Development
a7356.name: Dr. Thambo Gina
a7356.title: Eswatini Minister for Economic Planning and Development
a7356.speech: noted the country’s commitment to regional growth and industrialisation, stressing that targeted cooperation could accelerate development across the SADC region ; said Eswatini remained committed to the bloc’s shared objectives: “Our participation reflects Eswatini’s dedication to collaboration, sustainable development, and regional progress.”

a7356.speaker: SADC Council of Ministers
a7356.name: SADC Council of Ministers
a7356.speech: According to the Council, the SADC SMEs Competitiveness Strategy and the SADC Investment Climate Scorecard are expected to improve the region’s ability to attract capital, stimulate entrepreneurship, and compete in global markets.

a7356.speaker: SADC Council of Ministers
a7356.name: SADC Council of Ministers
a7356.speech: Ministers noted progress on several interconnector projects linking Angola, Malawi, and Tanzania to the Southern African Power Pool, which are expected to improve electricity reliability and reduce power deficits in multiple countries.

a7356.speaker: Elias Mpedi Magosi, SADC Executive Secretary
a7356.name: Elias Mpedi Magosi
a7356.title: SADC Executive Secretary
a7356.speech: confirmed that Madagascar had agreed to operationalise the SADC Centre for Renewable Energy and Energy Efficiency (SACREEE).

a7356.speaker: SADC Council of Ministers
a7356.name: SADC Council of Ministers
a7356.speech: Ministers noted that pooled procurement could lower costs, standardise quality, and strengthen supply chains for member states, especially in the face of health emergencies.

a7356.speaker: SADC Council of Ministers
a7356.name: SADC Council of Ministers
a7356.speech: The Council reported that US$206 million had been mobilised from International Cooperating Partners during the last financial year, but that US$624.5 billion is still required to implement priority projects under the Regional Indicative Strategic Development Plan (RISDP); Ministers stressed the need to broaden funding sources, including domestic resource mobilisation and public-private partnerships.

a7356.speaker: Elias Mpedi Magosi, SADC Executive Secretary
a7356.name: Elias Mpedi Magosi
a7356.title: SADC Executive Secretary
a7356.speech: said the Council’s work would feed directly into the Summit’s agenda: “The goal remains a peaceful, industrialised, and self-reliant Southern Africa.”

a7356.speaker: Eswatini Ministry of Economic Planning and Development
a7356.name: Eswatini Ministry of Economic Planning and Development
a7356.speech: According to the Ministry, Eswatini views the SADC Council of Ministers as a strategic platform to influence policy, secure investment opportunities, and strengthen partnerships that support the Kingdom’s economic goals.

a7356.speaker: Eswatini Ministry of Economic Planning and Development
a7356.name: Eswatini Ministry of Economic Planning and Development
a7356.speech: The Ministry confirmed that the delegation would present follow-up actions from the meeting to relevant stakeholders in Eswatini, ensuring alignment between national development plans and regional commitments.

a7361.speaker: Head of the Tete Provincial branch of the National Migration Service of Mozambique (SENAMI)
a7361.name: Head of the Tete Provincial branch of the National Migration Service of Mozambique (SENAMI)
a7361.speech: Told the International Organization for Migration (IOM) that the men, who were carrying no documents, have told SENAMI they are Ethiopians traveling to South Africa ; said the survivors are deeply traumatized and that the driver of the vehicle is in custody.

a7361.speaker: International Organization for Migration (IOM)
a7361.name: International Organization for Migration (IOM)
a7361.speech: Said it is coordinating with SENAMI to provide immediate assistance to the survivors, who are being treated for severe dehydration and exhaustion, including food and clothing.

a7361.speaker: International Organization of Migration (statistics)
a7361.name: International Organization of Migration (statistics)
a7361.speech: According to the International Organization of Migration every year more than 200,000 young Ethiopians crosses the country's border in search of better opportunities and exposed to wide range of risks.

a7361.speaker: IOM flow monitoring survey report on movement of Ethiopian migrants (released 18 March 2020)
a7361.name: IOM flow monitoring survey report on movement of Ethiopian migrants (released 18 March 2020)
a7361.speech: As the report stated the intended final destinations of migrants are further investigated for 3 specific reasons, namely travelling for job opportunities, ease of access to asylum procedures and ease of access to humanitarian assistance. Key findings show that most of the migrants surveyed, who was 69 percent male and 21 percent female, were unemployed. The primary country of departure amongst respondents was Ethiopia, followed by Sudan and Djibouti and the primary intended final destinations included the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, Sudan and Ethiopia.

a7361.speaker: United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs (UNDESA)
a7361.name: United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs (UNDESA)
a7361.speech: According to UNDESA, in 2019 South Africa was home to about 4.2 million migrants, and 290,000 asylum seekers and refugees. Zimbabwe, Somalia, Malawi, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Ethiopia were the main source countries.

a7392.speaker: Dr. Mohammed Goje, Executive Secretary, Yobe State Emergency Management Agency
a7392.name: Dr. Mohammed Goje
a7392.title: Executive Secretary, Yobe State Emergency Management Agency
a7392.speech: Said repositioning of the Agency to be data-driven was embarked upon having been appointed in 2019; speaking at a sideline event of the ongoing United Nations General Assembly in New York on Friday, he noted that data is non-negotiable when dealing with issues that border on both man-made and natural conflicts: “Prior to my appointment, I was a development worker with Clinton Health, managing Bill and Melinda Gates grants in Yobe State. When I took over in 2019, the first thing I did was to reform the Agency to be data-driven. When you are faced with man-made and natural conflict such as boko haram insurgency, flooding, fire and repatriation of IDPs that are in Camps, you must reposition yourself to work with data. So, I started repositioning the Agency to be data driven to ensure we have a reliable data we can work with.”

a7392.speaker: Dr. Mohammed Goje, Executive Secretary, Yobe State Emergency Management Agency
a7392.name: Dr. Mohammed Goje
a7392.title: Executive Secretary, Yobe State Emergency Management Agency
a7392.speech: Acknowledged that the withdrawal of funding by the Agency for International Development (USAID) left a huge gap in humanitarian response in Yobe State; noted that most of the partners complementing government's efforts are now having limited resources; assured that the government would not rest on its oars in filling the gap given that it is its primary responsibility to support and fund: “With the withdrawal of the USAID Funding, most of our partners that have keyed into complementing government's efforts have limited resources to support the ongoing response. But of course we did an analysis and there was a huge gap to fill because of the withdrawal of USAID Funding. Fortunately, there are some funds coming in through an international development partner. Even at that, the primary objective to support and fund lies with the government. Looking at our analysis, the government is looking at how to close the gap in terms of health, livelihood and other components of humanitarian responses.”
